lead.t: Varicose veins are abnormally dilated, tortuous superficial veins caused by increased intraluminal pressure and incompetent valves, rarely leading to embolism unlike deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

b: Definition: Abnormally dilated, tortuous superficial veins from prolonged increased intraluminal pressure causing progressive venous wall weakening and valve incompetence
Superficial veins of the leg affected in up to 20% of men and 33% of women
Also occur in: oesophagus (portal hypertension), anorectal region (haemorrhoids), spermatic cord (varicocele), broad ligament of uterus
Obesity, pregnancy (compress IVC), prolonged standing, familial predilection (familial valvular incompetence)
Pathophysiology: Elevated intraluminal pressure → venous wall dilation → valve incompetence → worsening venous stasis → more dilation (self-perpetuating cycle)

b: Abnormally dilated, tortuous veins produced by prolonged increased intraluminal pressure with vessel dilation and incompetence of venous valves
Superficial veins of the upper and lower leg most commonly involved — venous pressures in these sites can be elevated up to 10 times normal by prolonged dependent posture
Affect up to 20% of men and one third of women
Pregnancy — gravid uterus compresses inferior vena cava ↑ venous pressure; explains higher incidence in women
Familial predilection — reflects defective venous wall development

qs.q: A 58-year-old man presents with painful lower extremity swelling after a long international flight. Which complication specifically distinguishes deep vein thrombosis from superficial varicose veins?
o: Major risk of fatal pulmonary embolism
Local skin ulceration over the medial malleolus
qs.e: Deep vein thrombosis carries a high risk of life-threatening pulmonary embolism due to the large caliber of the vessels. In contrast, superficial varicose veins rarely cause pulmonary embolism because thrombi remain localized.

qs.q: A patient with longstanding varicose veins develops brownish discolouration and a non-healing ulcer above the medial malleolus. What is the correct term and mechanism for the skin discolouration?
o: Stasis dermatitis (brawny induration) from haemolysis of extravasated RBCs releasing haemosiderin
Chronic contact dermatitis from repeated venous compression bandaging
Erythema nodosum from immune complex deposition in venous endothelium
Lipodermatosclerosis from fat necrosis caused by venous hypertension
qs.e: Stasis dermatitis (brawny induration) results from chronic venous congestion → extravasation of RBCs → haemolysis → haemosiderin deposition → brawny discolouration and fibrosis.

qs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes superficial varicose veins from deep vein thrombosis regarding pulmonary embolism risk?
o: Both carry equal PE risk as thrombus can propagate freely between the vascular systems
DVT is the major source of PE; embolism from superficial varicose veins is very rare
Varicose veins carry higher embolism risk due to greater peripheral venous pressure
Neither causes PE without a concurrent cardiac septal defect allowing paradoxical emboli
qs.e: Embolism from superficial varicose veins is very rare. DVT — particularly in popliteal, femoral, and iliac veins — is the major source of potentially fatal pulmonary embolism.

ai.summary: Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous superficial veins caused by chronic venous hypertension and valve incompetence. They are common, especially in women, and can progress to chronic venous insufficiency.

sections.p: Varicose veins are visibly enlarged superficial veins, usually in the legs, diagnosed by clinical inspection and duplex ultrasound confirming reflux.

t.b: Does the vein have reflux? → Confirms venous insufficiency; normal flow rules out significant reflux.

sections.p: The CEAP classification grades clinical severity from C0 (no signs) to C6 (active ulcer). Staging guides treatment intensity.
Chronic venous hypertension from valve failure is primary; secondary causes increase pressure or damage valves.
b: Pelvic congestion (e.g., from pregnancy or portal hypertension)
Infections (e.g., lymphatic filariasis) in low‑resource settings

sections.p: Patients notice bulging, blue‑purple veins, heaviness, aching, and sometimes swelling after prolonged standing.
Focused imaging and labs identify reflux, rule out DVT, and detect contributing systemic disease.

t.b: Is there reflux or obstruction? → Positive reflux confirms diagnosis; no reflux suggests other causes.
Is arterial disease present? → Low ABI (<0.9) contraindicates compression therapy.
Is there infection or inflammation? → Elevated markers may indicate cellulitis or thrombophlebitis.

sections.p: Complications include chronic venous insufficiency, ulceration, superficial thrombophlebitis, and rare bleeding.
Treat underlying cause, use compression, and consider procedural correction when symptoms are moderate‑severe.
b: Compression stockings (30‑40 mmHg) to reduce venous pressure
Endovenous laser/ radiofrequency ablation for refluxing truncal veins

sections.p: Regular review of symptoms, skin, and ulcer healing; reinforce lifestyle measures to prevent progression.
b: Encourage weight control, activity, and avoidance of prolonged standing

sections.p: Conditions that mimic varicose veins may be mistaken for them.
b: Deep vein thrombosis (painful, swollen, not visible veins)

sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring or alarming.
b: Normal duplex does not exclude early reflux; repeat if symptoms persist
Compression may mask edema, hiding early skin changes

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden leg pain with warmth and swelling (possible DVT)
New ulcer or bleeding from a vein
Rapid increase in swelling or discoloration

faq.q: Can varicose veins cause blood clots?
faq.a: They rarely cause embolic events, but superficial thrombophlebitis can occur and should be treated.
No; many patients improve with compression and lifestyle changes; procedures are reserved for persistent symptoms or complications.

faq.q: Do pregnancy‑related varicose veins resolve after delivery?
faq.a: Often they improve, but some women retain veins and may need later treatment.
